land.text: San Ignacio Guazú, where three Jesuits began the first reduction in 1609 after the governor of Asunción 'made a deal with the Jesuit Provincial of Paraguay'; Guayrá followed within 22 years

predecessors.note: Cliopatria starts the row in 1595; the page's first reduction is 1609. The Guayrá land was Guaraní country that the page does not assign to a state.

land.text: the mission towns left after the expulsion: '89,000 Guaraní in 30 missions' passed to Spanish administration

successors.note: The page: 'In 1767, king Charles III of Spain expelled the Jesuits'; its population table marks 1768 'Jesuits expelled'. Cliopatria keeps the row to 1768.

capitals.name: San Ignacio Guazú
capitals.note: The first reduction (1609, present-day Paraguay). The missions had no capital; the Jesuit Provincial's seat (Córdoba) is not on the pages opened, so the first reduction stands for the state.

correction.text: from 1609 only (not 1595): the Paraguayan and Argentine reductions of the Cliopatria shape plus the Guayrá missions, 'the western two-thirds of present-day Paraná state ... more than 100,000 square kilometres'

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria 1595-1628, 215,783 km2: Paraguay 661 cells, Mato Grosso do Sul 120, Paraná 101 (about 26,000 km2, a quarter of the page's >100,000 km2 for Guayrá), Argentine Misiones 34. The page dates the first reduction to 1609 and the 15 Guayrá missions to 'the next 22 years', so 1595-1608 has no state. The page gives no infobox area for the whole. The Paraguayan part is unverified (page budget).

correction.text: for 1629-1631 only: the Cliopatria shape (with the Tapé missions of Rio Grande do Sul) plus Guayrá, which the bandeirantes were raiding from 1628; Guayrá drops out in 1632 (next keyframe)

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria 1629-1639, 261,430 km2, adds 74 cells of Rio Grande do Sul (the Tapé missions). Mbororé page: Raposo Tavares and Pires Preto raided Guayrá in 1628-1631 and the Tapé was 'invaded during the years 1636, 1637 and 1638'. The Tapé founding years are not on the pages (unverified: page budget).

correction.text: the Cliopatria 1629 shape without Paraná and Mato Grosso do Sul: 'By the year 1632, 12,000 Guarani had been forcibly moved south, leaving the Guayrá region virtually deserted'; the Tapé missions of Rio Grande do Sul remain until the 1636-1638 raids

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe. Main page: the Jesuits moved the Guayrá survivors from 1631 to 1638 about 500 km south-west 'into Spanish-controlled territory' (about 12,000 people). Itatín (Mato Grosso do Sul) was struck in 1632; the page says nothing of it afterwards, so it goes out with Guayrá (reading). Cliopatria keeps Paraná and Mato Grosso do Sul in the shape to 1756.

correction.text: the Cliopatria 1640 shape without Paraná and Mato Grosso do Sul: Guayrá and Itatín were abandoned, the missions lay on the Paraná and Uruguay in Paraguay and Argentine Misiones after the Guaraní victory at Mbororé on 11 March 1641

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria 1640-1737, 241,983 km2 (no Rio Grande do Sul). It still carries Guayrá (101 Paraná cells) and Itatín (120) although both were deserted by 1632. The Misiones Orientales page says that area 'formed part of the Jesuit Reductions' between 1609 and 1756 but gives no founding years for its seven towns, so the missing Rio Grande do Sul piece in 1640-1737 is left as Cliopatria has it (unverified: page budget).

correction.text: the Cliopatria 1738 shape without Paraná and Mato Grosso do Sul: the Paraguayan, Argentine and Misiones Orientales reductions at their peak population (141,242 in 1732)

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria 1738-1751, 261,430 km2: the Rio Grande do Sul piece (the Misiones Orientales, 74 cells) returns. The page's population peaks in 1732 (141,242; the introduction says 141,182). Paraná and Mato Grosso do Sul removed as in 1640.

correction.text: the Cliopatria 1752 shape without Paraná and Mato Grosso do Sul; the Misiones Orientales are still held although the Treaty of Madrid of 13 January 1750 gave them to Portugal, because the Guaraní refused to move

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria 1752-1756, 259,181 km2. The treaty page: Portugal was to receive 'seven independent Jesuit missions of the upper Uruguay River'; it cites 'the refusal of the Guaraní to be forcibly relocated'. The cession was carried out only after the Guaraní War (1756).

Cliopatria 1757-1762, 180,255 km2 (Paraguay 646 cells, Argentine Misiones 112, Corrientes 34): the shape of the corrected 1752 keyframe minus the Misiones Orientales. Guaraní War page: after Caiboaté 'the occupying forces forced the Guaraní to leave the missions ceded to Portugal'; Portugal held them to 1759, then Spain 'unilaterally ended' the treaty, and El Pardo (1761) returned them to Spain, but the page does not say the towns were refounded, and the Misiones Orientales page ends their Jesuit period in 1756.

correction.text: the shape unchanged, ending in 1767: 'In 1767, king Charles III of Spain expelled the Jesuits from the Spanish dominions in the Americas'

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria 1763-1768, 180,255 km2. Only the end year changes: the page leaves '89,000 Guaraní in 30 missions' in 1767 and lists 1768 as 'Jesuits expelled'; 1768 is the Cliopatria year, 1767 the page's sentence.

region.text: San Ignacio Guazú, in present-day Paraguay

ledger.note: 1609: three Jesuits begin the first reduction at San Ignacio Guazú. 'Three Jesuits began the first reduction in San Ignacio Guazú' after the governor of Asunción, 'acting under instructions from Philip III', made a deal with the Jesuit Provincial of Paraguay.

region.text: the Guayrá missions, 'covering the western two-thirds of present-day Paraná state' and 'more than 100,000 square kilometres'

ledger.note: 1609-1631: 15 missions in Guayrá. 'The Jesuits founded 15 missions in Guayrá over the next 22 years.' The page gives no year for each mission, so the span (1609 to about 1631) sits at its start; the page does not say which state held Guayrá.

region.text: the Guayrá missions raided by the São Paulo bandeirantes

ledger.note: 1628: the slave raids begin. 'Large-scale raids by the Bandeirante slavers of São Paulo on the missions and non-mission Guaraní began in 1628' (main page); Raposo Tavares and Pires Preto raided Guayrá in 1628-1631, taking about 5,000 people in 1628-1629 (Mbororé page). The raiders were São Paulo slavers; Portugal stands for Portuguese Brazil.

region.text: Guayrá, 'virtually deserted' after 12,000 Guaraní 'had been forcibly moved south', and Itatín, struck the same year

ledger.note: 1632: Guayrá is emptied. 'By the year 1632, 12,000 Guarani had been forcibly moved south, leaving the Guayrá region virtually deserted.' Main page: the Jesuits moved survivors from 1631 to 1638 about 500 km south-west into Spanish territory. The page does not say whether Itatín (Mato Grosso do Sul) was held afterwards.
1632: the Guayrá contest ends with the region deserted; the raiders turned to the Uruguay missions in 1636.

region.text: the Tapé, present-day Rio Grande do Sul

ledger.note: 1636: the bandeiras reach the Tapé. The Tapé was 'invaded during the years 1636, 1637 and 1638 by successive bandeiras' (André Fernandes, Fernando Dias Pais among the leaders); Diego de Alfaro led the Guaraní against them from late 1638.

region.text: the Tapé missions of Rio Grande do Sul

ledger.note: 1638: the Tapé missions are gone from the map. The page says the Tapé was invaded in 1636-1638 but 'does not explicitly say' the missions were destroyed; Cliopatria drops Rio Grande do Sul from the 1640 shape, and this bridges the silence.

region.text: the Uruguay and Paraná missions, with Cerro Mbororé near Panambí in Misiones

ledger.note: 11 March 1641: the Guaraní win at Mbororé. 'The battle ended in a Guarani victory': about 4,000 mission warriors under Nicolás Ñeenguirú against 450 bandeirantes and 2,700 Tupí auxiliaries; a Crown decree of 12 May 1640 allowed firearms 'if so directed by the prior Viceroy of Peru'.

region.text: the seven missions east of the Uruguay River (Misiones Orientales): San Miguel, Santo Ángel, San Lorenzo Mártir, San Nicolás, San Juan Bautista, San Luis Gonzaga, San Francisco de Borja

ledger.note: July 1754: Portuguese and Spanish troops march on the missions. The Treaty of Madrid (13 January 1750) gave the Misiones Orientales to Portugal; 'Spanish and Portuguese forces were sent in July 1754 to remove the Guaraní'; Sepé Tiaraju led the resistance and an armistice ended the year.

region.text: the seven missions east of the Uruguay River

ledger.note: July 1754: the Spanish side of the joint force (José de Andonaegui) acts against the Guaraní of its own missions to carry out the treaty.

region.text: the land east of the Uruguay River, 'including the seven missions', which 'went to Portugal'

ledger.note: February 1756: the Seven Missions fall. Sepé Tiaraju was killed on 7 February and at Caiboaté on 10 February '1,511 Guaraní were killed'; 'the occupying forces forced the Guaraní to leave the missions ceded to Portugal'. Portugal held them until 1759, when Spain 'unilaterally ended' the treaty; El Pardo (1761) annulled it with Spain 'regaining control over the seven missions'. Those Spanish regains are not Jesuit land in this dossier (the Misiones Orientales page ends their Jesuit period in 1756).

region.text: the seven missions east of the Uruguay River

ledger.note: 10 February 1756: Caiboaté, the last battle; 'a larger combined force of 3,000 Spanish and Portuguese troops crushed the revolt in 1756' (main page).

region.text: the seven missions east of the Uruguay River

ledger.note: 1756: the joint campaign ends in the defeat of the Guaraní revolt.

region.text: the remaining thirty missions, '89,000 Guaraní in 30 missions'

ledger.note: 1767: the Jesuits are expelled. 'In 1767, king Charles III of Spain (1759-88) expelled the Jesuits from the Spanish dominions in the Americas', leaving 89,000 Guaraní in 30 missions (78 Jesuits left); the population table has 88,864 in 1768, 'Jesuits expelled'. Cliopatria's last year is 1768.

wars.name: Bandeirante raids on the Guaraní missions (to the Battle of Mbororé)
wars.outcome: The bandeirantes emptied Guayrá (12,000 Guaraní moved south by 1632) and invaded the Tapé; the Guaraní militia 'defeated an army of 1,500 or more' at Mbororé on 11 March 1641 and the Uruguay and Paraná missions held.
wars.note: The page gives the Mbororé strengths as about 4,000 Guaraní against 450 bandeirantes and 2,700 Tupí auxiliaries, the main page 1,500 or more bandeirantes. The name is descriptive.

wars.name: Guaraní War

zones.text: the seven missions east of the Uruguay River (Misiones Orientales)

wars.outcome: Defeat of the Guaraní: Caiboaté on 10 February 1756, the Guaraní driven from the seven missions ceded to Portugal; the Treaty of Madrid was ended by Spain in 1759 and annulled by the Treaty of El Pardo in 1761.
wars.note: Infobox: July 1754 to February 1756; the main page says only 1756. The Treaty of Madrid (13 January 1750) page and the Guaraní War page agree on the cession.

certainty.note: Mission districts in forest and river country with no surveyed frontier; the Guayrá and Tapé extents are the page's descriptions.

The Treaty of Madrid (1750) made the Uruguay River the boundary of the Misiones Orientales ('the land east of it ... went to Portugal'), but it was never fixed on the ground (annulled 1761); everything else stays soft.

notes: Cliopatria's 1595 start is fourteen years before the first reduction (1609); the row carries Guayrá (Paraná) and Itatín (Mato Grosso do Sul) to 1756 although the pages say both were deserted by 1632 (Guayrá survivors moved 1631-1638), and drops the Misiones Orientales of Rio Grande do Sul in 1640-1737 although the Seven Missions were founded between 1682 and 1707 (not on the pages opened; a gap-filler should open 'Jesuit Reductions' or 'Misiones Orientales' history). The Tapé founding dates (1626-1634) are also not on the pages. Page budget (up to 5) was exceeded by one: the first Treaty of Madrid URL was a disambiguation page and the real article followed; a guess at 'Battle_of_Mbarori' returned not found. The Guaraní missions' relation to the Spanish crown (a protected, tribute-paying territory) was not recorded as vassalage because no page dates it. Several mission towns lie in Paraguay's Misiones and Itapúa and in Argentine Misiones and Corrientes; the Cliopatria shape is kept for them (unverified). The 'wars' names are descriptive; only the Guaraní War is a Wikipedia title. The 1767 date is the page's sentence, 1768 the Cliopatria end and the population table's expulsion year.
